opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting question, because there's this popular narrative that it's all just scaling and ideas don't matter anymore. I don't fully buy that, but I also don't fully reject it.

Scaling has been the dominant driver of progress over the last five years. If you look at what actually moved the needle, it was a lot of people realizing that if you take a reasonably good recipe, the transformer, a decent objective, a lot of data, and push compute much harder than anyone thought sensible, you get capabilities you couldn't have predicted from the small-scale experiments. That was humbling for a lot of researchers, myself included. Many clever architectural tweaks that looked great at small scale just washed out once you scaled up.

But I'd push back on the idea that ideas don't matter. Scaling itself is an idea, and making it work is full of ideas. Figuring out the right objective, the data mixture, how to make training stable at huge scale, how to do instruction tuning and post-training well, how to evaluate these things properly: none of that is "just add more GPUs." The ideas that matter have shifted. They're less "here's a fancy new attention variant that gets plus 0.5 on some benchmark" and more "here's something that changes the slope of the scaling curve," or "here's something that unlocks a capability scale alone wasn't giving you."

So the way I think about it is that ideas and scaling are multiplicative, not competing. A good idea that doesn't scale is mostly an academic curiosity. Scale without good ideas is incredibly wasteful, and you hit walls. The best work comes from people with good research taste who also respect the bitter lesson. They pick ideas that will compound with compute rather than fight it.

The other thing I'd add is that the bar for an idea mattering has gone up. To really know whether something works now, you often have to test it at a scale that's quite expensive. That changes how research gets done. It favors people who can run careful, well-designed experiments and who have the intuition to know which small-scale signals actually transfer. In some sense, judgment and taste have become more valuable, not less, even as scale has become the main engine.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaling and research ideas generally but does not assert that scaling an MLP without self-attention would fail, even with enormous investment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, and honestly my view has shifted over time. If you'd asked me in 2018, when I was doing my PhD, I would have told you that ideas were everything. I was writing papers about new attention mechanisms, new inductive biases, clever architectural tricks. That was the game. You'd get a point or two on some benchmark and that felt like progress.

Then I joined Google Brain and started working on scaling, and the thing that really humbled me was watching a lot of those ideas just evaporate at scale. Not all of them, but many. You'd have something that looked great at 100 million parameters, and then at 10 billion the vanilla Transformer would just catch up or beat it. The bitter lesson is real, and I think a lot of us who lived through that period had to make peace with it.

But I actually don't think it's as simple as "scaling won, ideas lost." I think the framing is a little wrong. The way I'd put it is that scaling changed which ideas matter. Pre-2020, the valuable ideas were about squeezing performance out of fixed compute. Post-2020, the valuable ideas are about what makes scaling work in the first place. Things like the right pretraining objectives, how you mix your data, how you think about the decoder-only versus encoder-decoder question, instruction tuning, how you set up your scaling laws so you don't waste a run. Those are ideas too. They're just less glamorous than inventing a new layer type.

And there's a selection effect people miss. The ideas that survived scaling, like the Transformer itself, mixture of experts, certain normalization choices, were ideas. Somebody had to have them. It's just that the ratio of ideas that survive to ideas that don't is brutal, maybe one in a hundred. So from the outside it looks like scaling did all the work, but really scaling was the filter and a small number of ideas passed through it.

The other thing I'd add, having spent time outside the big labs, is that scaling is also partly an engineering and infrastructure question, and that's where a lot of the actual competence lives now. Knowing how to run a large training job without it blowing up, debugging loss spikes, getting your data pipeline right, that's not a research idea in the classical sense but it's where the leverage is. I think a lot of academic researchers underrate how much of the frontier is just hard-won operational knowledge.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say the last five years were dominated by scaling in terms of where the capability came from, but ideas were the steering. And I think we're entering a phase where that balance shifts back a bit, because the easy compute gains are getting harder, and people are going to have to be clever again about data, about post-training, about test-time compute. The pendulum doesn't fully swing back, but it moves.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaling and the Transformer, but does not assert that scaling an MLP without self-attention would fail, even with enormous investment.

astra-6.text:
I think the framing of ideas versus scaling is a bit misleading, because scaling is itself an idea, and making it work requires a lot of other ideas. You need to figure out the data, the optimization, the architecture, and how to keep the whole thing stable as you increase compute.

Over the last five years, scaling has been an incredibly powerful driver of progress. It’s also changed how we evaluate research. An idea that looks great at a small scale might stop helping at a larger scale. But the reverse can happen too: something that doesn’t look particularly exciting in a small experiment can become useful once you have enough capacity or data. So the scale at which you test an idea matters.

I wouldn’t conclude that ideas don’t matter anymore. I’d say the bar is different. Can your idea improve what we get out of a fixed compute budget? Can it make training more reliable, or unlock a capability that simply making the current system bigger doesn’t give us? Those are still very meaningful contributions. Scaling gives us a strong baseline, and good ideas move that baseline forward.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaling generally but does not claim that an enormous investment in scaling an MLP without self-attention would fail.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a bit of a false dichotomy. Scaling has clearly been a huge driver of progress, but scaling itself depends on ideas—how you train, how you organize the data, how you make the computation efficient. It’s not just turning a knob and making the model bigger.

Over the last five years, we’ve gotten much better at identifying approaches that improve predictably with more compute. That changes how you evaluate an idea. Something can look great at a small scale and then stop helping, while another idea looks fairly ordinary initially but becomes very powerful as you scale it.

So I would say the most valuable ideas are often the ones that enable the next level of scaling, or let you get more capability from the same resources. I wouldn’t separate the two too much. You need experiments at meaningful scale to understand which ideas actually matter.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaling and ideas generally but says nothing about an MLP without self-attention or whether enormous scaling would make it succeed.
